News and Commentary Digital Travel Credentials: Seamless Travel or Major Headache?
 PUBLISHED October 29, 2026 AUTHOR Purdue Global Law School The U.S. and other authorities worldwide have been pushing the adoption of digital travel credentials. The goal is to streamline airline check-in and security screening. However, the technology faces significant legal and regulatory challenges.
 Digital travel credentials raise privacy concerns, questions of corporate surveillance, jurisdictional conflicts, and issues of border searches and seizures. Regulatory frameworks claim that digital ID programs are voluntary. However, travelers face pressure to adopt these new systems. Legal advocates argue that if opting out means facing long delays, missed flights, agent hostility, or extra fees, the consent may be considered legally coerced.
 Furthermore, digital ID programs don’t make travel seamless. Because there are no global interoperability standards, travelers must carry physical identification in case of problems with digital credentials.
 As a result, there is organized pushback against digital travel credentials from a broad coalition of privacy advocates, civil rights organizations, bipartisan lawmakers, and everyday travelers. As governments and airlines accelerate biometric checkpoints and smartphone ID integrations, resistance has formalized into lawsuits, legislative efforts, and public awareness campaigns.
 Airlines Lead the Push
 Airlines are pushing for digital credentials because they face financial and operational penalties when travel documents fail. If a traveler is turned away at check-in because of an expired passport or missing visa, it can cost airlines up to $16,000 in staff time, baggage removal, lost business, and reputational damage.
 The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has lobbied for digital identity systems to shift document verification upstream to the point of booking. The goal is to guarantee admissibility before the traveler sets foot in the airport.
 IATA’s standard, called One ID , is built on two legal and technical pillars. Rather than carrying physical travel documents, the traveler uses a digital identity app that securely communicates with the destination country’s immigration database. The government issues an encrypted “OK to Travel” token that the traveler sends to the airline.
 The airline replaces boarding passes and passport checks with facial biometrics. The traveler’s face becomes their token at bag drop, security, and the boarding gate. Airlines tout this process as seamless, contactless travel.
 Airline Pressure Drives Government Action
 The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have national security motives for implementing digital travel credentials. However, lobbying from the airline industry is a primary driver. Airlines view digital IDs as a financial and operational necessity to handle surging travel volumes.
 But the U.S. government isn’t starting from scratch. Agencies are stitching together statutory frameworks, administrative laws, and agency rulemakings that dictate how digital documents can be used at airport checkpoints. These rules reflect the interplay between state-level identification systems, privacy laws, and the rights of individual travelers.
 On top of this legal patchwork, a traveler must navigate a geopolitical and jurisdictional matrix at every step of their journey. While standing in the ticketing lobby, the traveler is protected by the Fourth Amendment and local and state laws governing privacy and police conduct. The moment they step into the TSA screening line, federal administrative rules take over.
 At the boarding gate, the traveler’s interaction with the airline is governed by the airline’s contract of carriage . While in the air, the traveler is suspended in the “transit cloud,” a jurisdictional twilight zone involving tech monopolies and the sovereign airspace of every country in the plane’s path, with minimal privacy or accountability. Upon landing, the traveler enters the jurisdiction of the host country’s border authority.
 A Privacy Minefield
 This jurisdictional handoff has privacy groups alarmed. A traveler cannot easily give informed, uncoerced consent to data sharing when the laws governing that data change several times over the course of a trip.
 Travelers also face legal risks related to border searches when carrying credentials on a mobile device. Immigration officials have the legal authority to search, copy, and detain phones and laptops at the border without a warrant. If a traveler’s device is seized as evidence, their identity is trapped inside it.
 Digital ID programs rely on corporations for technology, redirecting control of sensitive data and biometrics away from public accountability. Privacy advocates warn that this infrastructure can expose citizens to increased surveillance and excessive demands for data by private websites.
 Furthermore, sharing data with a third party can cause individuals to lose their Fourth Amendment expectation of privacy under U.S. law. Legal battles are brewing over whether transmitting a digital credential to an airline or a private biometrics company gives the government the right to access that data without a warrant.
 The Opt-Out Penalty: Time, Misinformation, and Passive Pressure
 Travelers retain the legal right to refuse digital identification and use a physical REAL ID or passport. Federal law mandates that REAL ID-compliant cards and passports remain acceptable.
 Federal law also protects a traveler’s right to opt out of facial recognition at TSA checkpoints. If a traveler opts into a biometric digital lane, federal regulations require the system to delete facial-scan metadata within 12 hours of identity verification. (CBP mandates biometrics for non-citizens with limited exceptions.)
 By law, international travelers cannot be penalized or denied entry for choosing the physical credential, but they will be directed to standard security or border control lines for manual processing. During peak hours, these lines are significantly longer. TSA’s website also states that domestic travelers who opt out of facial recognition will not be placed in another line or subjected to additional screening. However, they often face pushback and soft coercion.
 The Illusion of Seamless Travel
 Beyond privacy concerns, digital travel credentials can create headaches for travelers. The technology behind these systems has evolved over more than 2 decades . The International Civil Aviation Organization finalized its electronic passport specification in 2003. In 2021, the pandemic accelerated the adoption of contactless processing. Tech giants began integrating digital IDs into their wallet applications in 2022.
 This multi-decade progression explains why the technology can feel disjointed. Airlines and governments may use the word “seamless,” but travelers often face a fragmented, confusing, and stressful experience.
 A digital ID that works at a traveler’s home airport might not be accepted at their destination. Not all security lanes have the scanners needed to read digital credentials. Dead phone batteries, cracked screens, app crashes, or poor cell service can halt travel.
 Bottom line: TSA mandates that all passengers carry their physical ID as a backup.
 How Travelers Are Pushing Back
 In Congress, a bipartisan group of senators introduced the Traveler Privacy Protection Act to halt the TSA’s expansion of facial recognition. It seeks to force the TSA to provide highly visible opt-out signage, ban discriminatory treatment of passengers who opt out, strictly limit the storage of biometric data, and ban the use of TSA facial recognition for widespread surveillance. Major U.S. airlines and airport groups have stalled the legislation by claiming it would cause check-in delays and inflate staffing costs.
 To counter aggressive TSA officers who pressure travelers into biometric lanes, the Algorithmic Justice League (AJL) launched a public accountability campaign. The organization created a scorecard that allows travelers to log their airport experiences, report hidden or misleading opt-out signage, and document instances in which TSA agents illegally refused a physical ID.
 The greatest force against digital travel credentials may come from traveler skepticism and grassroots pushback. In an AJL study , 99% of participants said that TSA agents did not inform them of their right to decline the biometric scan. More than half felt unable or too uncomfortable to opt out because officers presented the process as mandatory.
 Navigating a Fragmented System
 Digital travel credentials involve aviation regulation, constitutional law, privacy statutes, and international agreements, and no single legal framework currently governs the full experience of a traveler's journey. Travelers and advocates who push back against biometric checkpoints today are shaping how — and whether — these systems get built with meaningful consent and oversight.
